plot_extraction.response_text:
Sam Lawson tells two boys about a local attempt to recover Captain Kidd’s buried treasure. According to legend, a marked rock by the river conceals a fortune guarded by the spirits of people Kidd murdered. Impoverished Mother Hokum urges her husband to organize a dig with Toddy Whitney, Harry Wiggin, and Primus King, an expert laborer who wisely demands payment in advance. Sam accompanies them but refuses a share, believing the treasure is cursed.

At midnight under a full moon, Primus digs beneath the rock while Sam warns everyone that they must remain silent if they find the treasure or it will disappear. The men uncover what seems to be a large iron pot and begin hauling it from the hole. Just as it reaches the surface, Toddy excitedly announces that they have it. The rope snaps, the pot apparently sinks deep into the earth, and a terrifying laugh is heard.

Sam admits that he slept through the crucial event and saw none of it himself. He awakens to find Hokum fighting Toddy for ruining their chance, while Primus laughs because he has already secured his payment. The disappointed men fill in the hole, and Sam concludes that losing the treasure spared them from its curse, though he cannot say what—if anything—the pot contained.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a nineteenth-century regionalist, oral-tale style, combining a polished frame narrative with an extended vernacular monologue. The opening narration is leisurely and pictorial, establishing the barn as an idyllic, secluded storytelling place through long, balanced sentences and abundant sensory detail: fragrant hay, autumn light, murmuring hens, riverbanks, elms, and water-lilies. This pastoral calm creates a drowsy, nostalgic atmosphere and frames the ensuing legend as communal entertainment remembered from childhood. The first-person plural viewpoint—“we”—gives the frame an intimate, collective quality, while occasional first-person singular interjections make the listeners active participants in the tale.

The dominant voice is Sam Lawson’s, rendered through heavily phonetic rural New England dialect. Nonstandard spellings and contractions such as “Wal,” “jest,” “suthin’,” “arter,” “crittur,” and “goin’” reproduce pronunciation and make the prose sound performed rather than written. His speech is repetitive, digressive, and formulaic. He repeatedly begins passages with “Wal” or “Lordy massy,” addresses his audience as “boys,” and uses conversational fillers such as “ye see” and “kind o’.” These verbal habits supply rhythm, characterize him immediately, and allow the narrative to wander through anecdotes, moral reflections, local gossip, and supernatural lore. The children’s impatient questions repeatedly redirect him, creating a comic tension between their desire for plot and his pleasure in delay.

Syntax varies sharply between the two narrative levels. The frame narrator favors elaborate, grammatically controlled sentences with descriptive clauses, lists, and literary comparisons. Sam’s syntax is looser and additive, often chaining events with “and,” repeating words for emphasis, or shifting direction mid-thought. His storytelling relies on incremental phrasing—“they drawed and they drawed,” “down, down, down,” “tried and tried and tried”—which imitates spoken emphasis and heightens suspense. Dialogue is frequently nested inside his account, so that Sam not only tells the story but impersonates Mother Hokum, Primus, and the treasure hunters. This gives the episode the lively quality of a dramatic performance.

The tone blends nostalgia, rustic comedy, mock solemnity, and mild supernatural suspense. Sam continually turns sensational material into moral instruction, treating Captain Kidd’s fate as a warning against rejecting religion or “hastin’ to be rich.” Yet his moral authority is gently undermined by his evasions, laziness, self-interest, and carefully qualified involvement in the treasure hunt. He insists that his conscience kept him from participating while admitting that he accompanied the group, advised them on supernatural procedure, concealed his purpose from his wife, and conveniently slept through the decisive event. This gap between his self-presentation and his conduct is the story’s central comic irony.

The narrative is deliberately digressive. The promised account of buried treasure is postponed by a ballad, a summary of Captain Kidd’s career, the history of the Hokum family, an anecdote about an unpaid butcher’s bill, arguments about poverty and wealth, drinking, ghost stories, and a description of divining rods. These apparent detours build a dense portrait of village culture, where folklore, religious teaching, social resentment, rumor, and practical cunning coexist. The plot itself follows the shape of a folk legend: a marked rock, treasure guarded by spirits, a prescribed rule of silence, a midnight excavation, a tantalizing discovery, and a fatal spoken exclamation that causes the treasure to vanish.

Humor arises from exaggeration, incongruity, repetition, and anticlimax. Mother Hokum’s enormous family is described through comic images such as a “rabbit-pen” with a “tow-head to every crack and cranny,” while the treasure hunters loudly deny belief in spirits as they fortify themselves with alcohol. Primus is the most practically intelligent participant: he demands payment in advance, secures it before the expedition, and laughs when the others lose their imagined fortune. The final revelation that Sam did not actually see the pot because he fell asleep punctures the supernatural climax and leaves the entire event suspended between legend, drunken misperception, and comic fabrication.

Imagery shifts with the mood. The opening uses soft, graceful, pastoral imagery, while the midnight section introduces blood-red leaves, answering whippoorwills, whispering trees, hollow grave-like sounds, groans, and buried corpses. Sound is especially important: hens “craw, crawing,” Caesar’s fiddle, the lugubrious pirate ballad, the spade striking iron, the snapped rope, the descending “jink, jink, jink,” and the final unearthly laugh. These auditory details reinforce the sense that the story belongs to oral culture and is designed to be heard.

The prose also incorporates songs, proverbial expressions, biblical language, sermonizing, and literary allusion. The Captain Kidd ballad interrupts the prose with repetitive verse and supplies a miniature moral biography of rebellion, murder, and punishment. Phrases such as “vanity,” “judgment day,” “ways o’ sin,” and “the Devil’s money” reflect a community steeped in Protestant moral vocabulary, though Mother Hokum’s complaint about the prosperous parson introduces social satire and exposes the economic distance between religious instruction and poverty.

Characterization is largely achieved through voice. Sam is leisurely, evasive, superstitious, self-excusing, and theatrically moralistic. Mother Hokum is forceful, resourceful, irreverent, and driven by material hardship. The treasure hunters are credulous, lazy, and greedy, whereas Primus is skeptical and financially shrewd. The frame narrator’s amused treatment encourages readers to enjoy these figures as village types. At the same time, the portrayals of Black characters rely on period racial terminology, stereotype, caricatured dialect, and generalized racial commentary. These elements are integral to the historical style but mark the story’s perspective as paternalistic and racially dated.

Overall, the style is expansive, performative, and gently satirical. Its chief effects come less from the buried-treasure plot than from the contrast between elegant narration and rustic speech, the storyteller’s comic unreliability, the accumulation of local detail, and the transformation of village gossip into folklore. The ending remains characteristically inconclusive: rather than resolving whether the treasure existed, it returns to Sam’s amused impatience with questioning, preserving the ambiguity and sociable charm of a tale whose real subject is the act of storytelling itself.

generation.response_text:
The upper bay of Grandfather’s barn was our chosen country on those long, mellow afternoons when September had begun to lay a yellow finger here and there upon the maples, though summer still lingered in the hollows and along the river. There the hay, sweetened by months of darkness and warm weather, rose in fragrant cliffs on either hand; through the broad door we saw the low meadow, with its silver threads of water, its clumps of purple aster, and its ranks of elms standing as grave and peaceful as a congregation at prayer. Below us the hens went murmuring among the chaff, now and then breaking into a confidential “craw, craw,” as if some matter of importance had been settled; and from the orchard came the lazy dropping of apples, each with a soft thud that made the silence seem deeper.

It was there that Sam Lawson found us one afternoon, my brother and me, lying upon the hay and watching motes turn slowly in the bars of sunlight.

Sam had come ostensibly to mend a rake-handle, but as he had brought neither knife, wedge, nor hammer, and as he sat down at once with his back against a beam, we understood that Providence had designed him for other employment.

“Sam,” said my brother, “did Captain Kidd ever bury any money along our river?”

Sam looked at us for some moments with the deliberate pity which age bestows upon youth when youth happens by accident to approach an interesting subject too directly.

“Wal, boys,” said he, “there’s them that says he did, and there’s them that says he didn’t; and them that says he didn’t mostly never went arter it, so their testimony ain’t wuth so much as t’ other sort. A man can set by his kitchen fire and say there ain’t no bears in the North Woods; but that don’t alter the tracks in the snow.”

“Were there tracks?” I asked.

“Not bear-tracks,” said Sam. “Money-tracks. Signs. Marks on rocks. Dreams. Divinin’-rods that would turn in a man’s hand like a trout on a line. And there was old Aunt Nabby Pease, that woke up three nights runnin’ with the taste o’ silver dollars in her mouth. That’s a cur’ous circumstance, though Nabby did take calomel frequent, and calomel will do sing’lar things to folks.”

“But did you ever dig for Kidd’s treasure?”

“Me? Lordy massy, no!” said Sam, with virtuous warmth. “I never dug for no treasure. I was present when some misguided critturs undertook suthin’ o’ that natur’; but I didn’t have no share in it. Wouldn’t. Not for kingdoms. ‘Hastin’ to be rich,’ Scriptur’ says, ‘pierces a man through with many sorrers,’ or words to that amount. I allers held that money come by honest labor was the only money a man could lay his head down alongside of and sleep peaceful.”

My brother glanced at Sam’s hands, which bore no signs of recent conflict with honest labor, but he prudently asked only, “Who did dig?”

“Wal,” said Sam, settling deeper into the hay, “to begin at the beginnin’, ye’ve got to know suthin’ about Cap’n Kidd.”

“We know about him.”

“No, ye don’t,” said Sam. “Boys never know nothin’ complete. They know the middle and want the end, but the beginnin’ they despise, though that’s commonly where the moral lays hid.

“Kidd was a respectable seafarin’ man to start with, so I’ve heerd. Wore good broadcloth of a Sunday, give to the poor when folks was lookin’, and could say grace to a dinner without peekin’ under his eyelids to see who got the breast o’ the chicken. Then he took to piracy. It was gradual, I s’pose. Sin mostly is. Fust a little suthin’ that don’t seem to signify; then another little suthin’; then, afore ye know it, ye’re sailin’ under a black flag with a knife in your teeth and the judgment day astarn of ye.”

Sam paused, folded his arms, and began in a cracked, melancholy chant:

> “My name was Captain William Kidd,  
> As I sailed, as I sailed;  
> Much wickedly I surely did,  
> As I sailed.  
>   
> “I struck a man and laid him low,  
> And where he sleeps no soul may know;  
> The tide comes in, the tide goes out,  
> And ghosts they walk the sands about—  
> As I sailed.”

“That isn’t all the song,” I said.

“No,” replied Sam; “and it’s a mercy. Caesar Peters used to fiddle thirty-seven verses of it at muster-time, and every verse was more discouragin’ than the one afore. There was one about his mother, and one about the gallows, and one about Satan waitin’ on the wharf. Caesar could draw that fiddle-bow acrost the strings till it sounded like a rusty gate swingin’ in a graveyard wind.

“Wal, Kidd sailed up and down, robbin’ ships and murderin’ folks, and when he got more gold than was convenient to carry, he buried it. That’s reasonable. Gold is heavy, boys. Folks that ain’t got none thinks it’s light as vanity, but them that has it knows better. He’d come ashore by night with a crew and a chest, and choose a likely place—a p’int, or a big tree, or a rock with a mark on it. Then he’d make one o’ the crew dig the hole. When the hole was done and the money in, Kidd would kill the digger and put him atop of it.”

“What for?”

“To guard it.”

“A dead man couldn’t guard it.”

Sam turned upon me almost severely.

“Couldn’t he? Then why don’t folks go alone through buryin’-grounds at midnight? A live watchman has to be paid, and he may go to sleep or take to drink; but a spirit will stay by treasure a hundred year, and never ast for higher wages. Kidd was a forehanded man in some respects.”

The particular hoard about which we had asked, Sam continued, was believed to lie under a great gray stone on the riverbank, two miles above the village. It was a lonely place even at noon. The river there narrowed between steep banks; ancient hemlocks leaned over the water, and the roots of a blasted pine gripped the earth like the claws of some buried animal. Upon the stone itself were three marks: a cross, a crooked line, and a hollow shaped like the print of a thumb.

“Now,” said Sam, “some allowed the cross meant religion, which Kidd hadn’t ought to have trifled with; some said it stood for ten thousand pounds; and old Deacon Barlow said the crooked line meant the ways o’ sin. But Mother Hokum said it was a shovel.”

“Who was Mother Hokum?”

“Wal, she was Hokum’s wife,” said Sam, as if the information were exhaustive. “Folks called her Mother because she had enough children to mother the county. Their house was a little brown concern back o’ the mill, with a roof that sagged in the middle and a winder propped up by a hymn-book. There was a tow-head to every crack and cranny. Look into the woodshed, and there’d be two young Hokums settin’ in a meal-barrel; lift the bedquilt, and like as not there’d be another asleep crossways at the foot. It put ye in mind of a rabbit-pen.

“Hokum himself was a mild, mournful man, with great ideas and poor execution. He could tell how to farm twenty acres, but couldn’t raise beans on one. He was allers jest goin’ to do suthin’. Monday he was goin’ to mend the fence; Tuesday he was goin’ to hire out; Wednesday he’d heard of a dog that could smell out copper mines, and by Thursday he was calculatin’ what he’d do with his profits.

“Mother Hokum, she took in washin’, spun wool, braided hats, nursed sick folks, and kep’ the family from droppin’ through the bottom of creation. She’d a tongue in her head, too. Parson Lothrop called once and told her poverty was a blessed discipline.

“‘So I’ve heerd,’ says she, wringin’ out a sheet, ‘but I notice the Lord mostly gives that discipline to them that’s got no choice, while you and Mis’ Lothrop are permitted to struggle along with two cows, a hired gal, and a smoke-house full o’ pork.’

“The parson says riches was vanity.

“‘Then,’ says she, ‘I wish Hokum had vanity enough to pay the butcher.’

“That butcher’s bill was an old affliction. Abner Sykes had sent it eleven times. The twelfth time Mother Hokum took the paper, folded it into a little boat, and set it sailin’ down the brook.

“‘There,’ says she, ‘if Abner wants his money, he can foller it to sea. Maybe Cap’n Kidd’ll pay him.’

“And that’s what set her thinkin’.”

“About the treasure?” my brother prompted.

“Jest so. She’d heard of the marked rock, same as everybody had. There was a divinin’-woman over in East Parish who said the money was there, and there was a red-haired pedler that dreamed of an iron pot three nights runnin’. Red hair is powerful for dreams, though uncertain in business. Then one fall Hokum got uncommon low. No corn, no pork, no shoes for half the children, and a note comin’ due at the bank. Mother Hokum stood him up by the woodpile.

“‘Hokum,’ says she, ‘you’ve talked about that treasure for fifteen year. Now you go and git it.’

“‘But, Mariar,’ says he, ‘it may be guarded.’

“‘You’ve got nine children,’ says she. ‘What’s one ghost more?’

“‘Diggin’s hard work.’

“‘Then git somebody that knows how.’

“So Hokum went to Toddy Whitney and Harry Wiggin. Toddy was called Toddy not because that was his lawful name, but on account of a drink he admired. He didn’t believe in spirits—not spirits without bottles, leastways—but he’d seen lights by the marked rock. Harry Wiggin had once found a counterfeit fourpence in a field and had considered himself gifted for treasure ever since. Both of ’em entered into the scheme hearty.

“But when it came to diggin’, Toddy had rheumatiz in his shoulder, Harry had a weak back, and Hokum was needed to direct. So they went after Primus King.”

Sam’s manner changed slightly when he spoke of Primus; there was in it the reluctant respect of an impractical man for one whom no amount of moonshine could deprive of common sense.

“Primus,” he said, “was the best hand with pick and spade in these parts. Strong, steady, and no more scared of a graveyard than he was of a turnip-patch. He listened while Hokum told about Kidd, the iron pot, the murdered sailor, and the ten thousand pounds.

“‘What do I get?’ says Primus.

“‘A share,’ says Hokum.

“‘A share of what?’

“‘Of the treasure.’

“‘Have you seen it?’

“‘Not yet.’

“‘Then I’ll take two dollars now.’

“Hokum argued and Toddy argued. Harry said it showed a want of faith. Primus says, ‘Faith don’t buy flour. Two dollars before I lift the spade.’

“‘But s’pose we find a million?’ says Toddy.

“‘Then you can afford the two dollars,’ says Primus.

“Mother Hokum heard of it, took the last money from the blue teapot, and paid him herself. That was wisdom. Whatever happened after, Primus’s treasure was already dug up.”

“And you went too?” I asked.

“Wal—not as a participator,” said Sam. “I went in a advisory capacity. Hokum come to me because I’d read considerable about supernatural manifestations, and because my great-uncle Peleg had owned a divinin’-rod.”

“Did the rod work?”

“It worked at turnin’,” said Sam. “Only trouble was, it turned jest as well over old boots as over silver. Uncle Peleg dug up seven boots, a stove-lid, and the skeleton of a cat, and then Aunt Jerushy chopped the rod for kindlin’.

“I told Hokum plain that buried money was Devil’s money. Spirits don’t take kindly to bein’ disturbed; and if Kidd had put a murdered man there, why, that man might feel he’d acquired rights in the property. I warned him.

“‘Sam,’ says Hokum, ‘you needn’t take a share.’

“‘I won’t,’ says I.

“‘But you might come along,’ says he, ‘and tell us what not to do.’

“That appeared Christian. A man may properly keep others from danger, even if it carries him two miles from home at midnight. I didn’t tell Mis’ Lawson exactly where I was goin’, because women are apt to confuse caution with superstition. I said I was settin’ up with a sick friend. Hokum was sick with poverty, and Toddy was commonly sick with suthin’, so it wa’n’t no lie in the gross, though perhaps it might have been improved in particulars.”

The night appointed was the last full moon of October. All day the sky had been pale and windless, and toward evening the frost sharpened the air. After supper, while the village settled into darkness and one kitchen light after another disappeared, the five men assembled behind Hokum’s woodshed.

Primus brought his tools. Harry brought a lantern, though they had agreed not to use it unless the moon failed. Toddy brought a stone jug, declaring that a swallow now and then was excellent against night vapors. Hokum brought a coil of rope, two sacks, and a list, prepared by Mother Hokum, of debts to be paid from the treasure.

“She’d put everything down,” said Sam, “from Abner’s butcher’s bill to a new meetin’-house bonnet. There was even ‘Hokum, a decent coat—if money remains.’ She understood his habits.

“We started nigh eleven. The moon was big and white over the east hill, and the leaves, what was left of ’em, shone red as old blood. The road was tolerable cheerful, but when we turned into the river path, the trees begun whisperin’ among themselves. There wa’n’t wind enough to stir a candle, but them trees whispered. Then a whippoorwill called on one side of us, and another answered from t’other.

“Harry says, ‘That’s a warnin’.’

“Toddy says, ‘Nonsense,’ and took a drink against it.

“Presently we come to the rock. Boys, it looked twice as big by moonlight. The mark on it wa’n’t a shovel then, nor a cross neither. It looked like a man with his head cut off.”

Sam paused until even the hens below seemed to listen.

“Now,” he resumed, “there’s rules in treasure-diggin’. Fust, ye mustn’t speak when once the spade goes in. Second, ye mustn’t answer if anything calls your name. Third, ye mustn’t look behind ye, no matter what comes. Most important of all, when the treasure shows, not one livin’ soul must say a word till it’s safe above ground. If ye speak, it’ll sink. That’s been proved time and ag’in.

“I explained all that. Toddy asked if whisperin’ counted. I said it did. Harry asked if groanin’ counted. I said likely it depended who groaned. Hokum asked what to do if the ghost attacked us. Primus drove his spade into the earth and said, ‘You hired me to dig. You gentlemen can settle the ghost.’

“Then we begun—or Primus begun. The rest of us stood round and assisted by lookin’ solemn.

“The dirt was tough with roots. Primus cut through ’em, steady as a clock. Chunk—scrape—thump. Chunk—scrape—thump. Every shovelful made the hole deeper, and every sound went rollin’ through the woods as if somebody under the ground was knockin’ back.

“After a spell the moon went behind a cloud. The river turned black, and a noise come up from it like a man drawin’ a long breath.

“Hokum edged near me.

“‘Sam,’ says he—forgettin’ the rule already—‘what’s that?’

“I wouldn’t answer. I jest pointed at the river.

“Toddy whispered, ‘Bullfrog.’

“Then suthin’ went who-o-o through the hemlocks.

“Harry grabbed my arm.

“‘That’s him,’ says he.

“‘Who?’ says Toddy.

“‘The murdered sailor.’

“Primus kept diggin’.

“‘Murdered sailors seem uncommon fond of owls,’ says he.

“At that Toddy laughed, but it wa’n’t a free laugh. Then he took another drink and declared he didn’t believe in ghosts, not one mite. Harry said neither did he. Hokum said he’d allers considered such things contrary to reason. And every one of ’em crowded nearer Primus.

“Down he went—down, down, down—till only his head and shoulders showed above the hole. We heard the spade strike stones, roots, gravel. Once it struck suthin’ hollow.

“Jink!

“Everybody stopped breathin’.

“Primus tried it again.

“Jink—jink!

“Boys, there’s no sound in this world like iron under a spade at midnight when ye’re expectin’ ten thousand pounds. It goes right through the ear and lays hold of the covetous part of the heart.

“Hokum dropped on his knees by the hole. Harry’s teeth begun to chatter. Toddy’s eyes looked as big as saucers.

“Primus cleared away the dirt with his hands. Presently he says, very low, ‘There’s something here.’

“I reminded him by signs that he mustn’t speak.

“He looked up and says, ‘Then how am I to tell you where to put the rope?’

“That was reasonable. Rules has to bend to circumstances.

“They lowered the lantern into the hole, with a coat thrown over it so the light wouldn’t attract spirits—or constables, for there was some question whose land we was on. We could see the curved black side of suthin’ big. Iron it looked to be. Primus scraped and scraped. There was a rim, and under the rim a kind of handle.

“An iron pot?” my brother cried.

“So it appeared,” said Sam. “A great iron pot, or kittle, or chest with rounded sides. They got the rope under the handle and hauled. It didn’t stir.

“They hauled again. Primus pried below with the pick, while Hokum, Toddy, and Harry pulled above. I stood apart.”

“Why didn’t you help?”

“Conscience,” said Sam. “Besides, there wa’n’t room on the rope.

“They tried and tried and tried. The rope strained. The handle creaked. The earth around the pot cracked loose, and from far off—or maybe from under our feet—come a groan.

“Hokum let go.

“Primus says, ‘Take hold.’

“Hokum took hold.

“Then they drawed and they drawed. Up come the pot an inch. Then another inch. Dirt rattled off it. Suthin’ inside went chink—soft and heavy. Coin, boys. Or pebbles. Pebbles will chink if they’re situated right, but nobody thought of that then.

“The moon come out sudden, shinin’ straight into the hole. There was the rim of the pot, risin’—risin’—and the rope stretched thin and hard.

“Hokum’s face was purple. Harry was prayin’ without makin’ a sound. Toddy had both feet braced against the rock. Primus stood below, heavin’ upward with his shoulder.

“Up it come—slow, slow—till the rim was level with the ground.

“And then Toddy Whitney hollered:

“‘We’ve got it!’

“At that instant the rope snapped.”

Sam clapped his hands sharply. We both started.

“Down went the pot. Jink! It struck once. Then again, deeper. Jink—jink—jink—down, down, down, as though the earth had opened its mouth and was swallowin’ it. The bottom fell out of the hole—or seemed to—and there come a laugh.

“Not a human laugh. No, sir.

“It begun low, under the roots: ‘Ho—ho—ho!’ Then it run along the bank and acrost the river and up among the trees, louder and louder, till the whole night appeared to be laughin’ at ’em.

“‘Ha—ha—ha-a-a!’

“Toddy fell backward. Harry went over the rock on all fours. Hokum jumped into the hole and clawed at the dirt with his hands. Primus climbed out considerable prompt.”

“What did you do?” I asked.

“Me?” Sam looked offended by the personal turn of the question. “I maintained myself as well as could be expected.”

“Did you hear the laugh?”

“Wal—now we’re comin’ to a p’int that needs explainin’.”

He removed a straw from his sleeve, examined it, and let it fall.

“Ye see, boys, I hadn’t slept well the night afore. Mis’ Lawson had been dryin’ apples, and the young one had the croup, and our brindle cow had got out about two in the mornin’. Then the walk, and the night air, and Toddy’s—well, never mind that—and standin’ still while Primus dug, all had a soothin’ effect.

“There was a soft place under the hemlock, banked with leaves. I set down there merely to meditate on the vanity of riches. And meditation, when pursued earnest, sometimes passes into sleep without a man bein’ aware of the exact boundary.

“So, strictly speakin’, I didn’t see the pot come up.”

“You were asleep!” my brother exclaimed.

“Not through the whole operation,” said Sam. “I seen the beginnin’, and I seen the consequences. A witness ain’t disqualified because he closes his eyes during portions not essential to his moral judgment.”

“Then you didn’t hear the laugh either?”

“I woke up with it—or with Hokum and Toddy makin’ a noise that might account for part of it. There’s owls, too, and echoes. I don’t undertake to say. A prudent man don’t explain more than Providence reveals.”

When Sam awoke, as he told us, the moon was shining peacefully over a scene in which peace had no other representative. Hokum had Toddy by the collar and was endeavoring to shake him apart.

“‘You spoke!’ Hokum says. ‘You opened your everlastin’ mouth!’

“‘How’d I know?’ says Toddy.

“‘Sam told ye.’

“‘Sam was asleep!’

“‘That don’t alter the rule!’

“Harry was kneelin’ by the hole, callin’ down into it, ‘Come back! Come back!’ which was foolish, because if it was treasure, it wouldn’t obey, and if it was a spirit, ye didn’t want it to.

“Primus sat on the marked rock laughin’.

“Hokum turned on him.

“‘What you laughin’ at?’

“Primus jingled the two dollars in his pocket.

“‘My treasure didn’t sink,’ says he.

“That made Hokum madder. He said everybody had cheated him—Toddy by speakin’, Harry by not pullin’ strong enough, Primus by havin’ no faith, and me by sleepin’ when I ought to have been advisin’.

“‘You told me I wa’n’t to have no share,’ says I. ‘A man can’t be expected to stay awake over property he’s renounced.’

“We searched the hole at daylight. Primus dug another three feet, cash in advance for the extra work. There wa’n’t no pot. There wa’n’t even a bottom such as had been there. The earth was packed and stony, jest common earth, with one old horseshoe in it and a piece of black root.

“Toddy said the root was what they’d taken for a handle. Harry said the treasure had sunk to the center of the world. Hokum said Kidd had removed it out of spite. Primus said nothing, because a man with four dollars has less need of opinions.

“They filled the hole. That took till breakfast-time. Men are allers slower puttin’ earth back than takin’ it out, particularly when there ain’t no fortune under it.

“When Hokum got home, Mother Hokum met him at the door. She looked at his clothes, his empty sacks, and his face.

“‘Did ye get it?’ says she.

“‘Toddy spoke,’ says Hokum.

“She never asked another question. She took the treasure list, turned it over, and wrote on the back an advertisement for washin’.”

“And was the iron pot truly there?” I persisted.

Sam gazed out of the barn door. The sunlight had climbed the opposite wall, and over the meadow the shadows of the elms stretched long and blue. A hen below us announced, with sudden pride, the discovery of something beneath the straw.

“Wal,” he said at last, “Hokum swore to it till the day he died. Harry swore to it when sober. Toddy swore both ways, accordin’ to whether he felt blamed. Primus said he dug up something heavy, but whether it was Kidd’s gold, an old kittle, or the natural hardness of the earth, he wouldn’t undertake to decide for no man.

“As for me, I seen enough to know that treasure-seekin’ is vanity. If they’d got that money, it would have brought quarrels, lawsuits, extravagance, and maybe the murdered sailor along with it. Hokum might have took to high livin’; Toddy surely would; Harry would have dug up the whole township. Mother Hokum alone might have made sensible use of it, but riches has strange ways even with sensible folks.

“So I’ve allers held we was mercifully delivered.”

“But,” said my brother, “you didn’t get anything at all.”

Sam rose slowly, brushing the hay from his coat.

“Wal, boys,” he replied, “I got home in time for breakfast, and I got the story. Money spends and is gone; but a good story improves with keepin’.”

He moved toward the ladder, then paused and looked back at us.

“Only,” he added, “if ye ever tell it, be particular to say I never dug. I merely went along to keep them poor critturs from doin’ anything foolish.”

Then he descended into the dimness below, where the hens received him with low, skeptical murmurs; and we remained in the fragrant hay, looking beyond the elms toward the unseen river, unable to determine whether Captain Kidd’s pot had sunk into the earth, or whether it had never risen anywhere except in the rich and inexhaustible country of Sam Lawson’s remembrance.

# The Mapmaker’s Last Island

On the morning the island disappeared, Mara Venn was drawing its western cliffs.

She sat at her worktable beneath the lighthouse windows, surrounded by sharpened pencils, bottles of ink, and the quiet instruments of her trade. A brass compass lay open beside her elbow. A pair of dividers rested on a sheet of ivory paper. Outside, gulls wheeled through the mist, crying as if they had misplaced something important.

Mara dipped her pen and traced the coastline from memory.

Blackhook Point first: a crooked horn of stone reaching into the northern sea. Then the long curve of Fisherman’s Bay, where the water turned green over pale sand. South of that lay the village, the orchards, the ruined watchtower, and the road that climbed toward the lighthouse in twelve narrow bends.

She knew every wall, path, and weathered roof on the island. For thirty-seven years she had made maps of places other people had forgotten to remember.

But that morning, when she looked through the eastern window, there was no island below her.

There was only sea.

Mara blinked.

The lighthouse stood upon its rocky hill as always, but the hill itself seemed to end a few yards beyond the door. Where the village should have rested in the valley, gray water moved under gray sky. No church bell. No chimneys. No orchards. No road curling upward from the harbor.

She rose so quickly that her chair fell backward.

The lighthouse door opened onto a ledge slick with mist. Waves lapped at the edge. The lower half of the tower—foundations, cellar, and all—should have been buried in solid rock, yet the sea now surrounded it as if the lighthouse were the final tooth in a drowned giant’s jaw.

“Mara?”

She turned.

Her apprentice, Eli, stood halfway down the spiral stairs, carrying two cups of tea. He was seventeen, long-limbed, untidy, and almost always hungry. His dark hair looked as though he had been sleeping in a high wind.

He saw the open door.

One cup slipped from his hand and shattered.

For a while, neither of them spoke.

Then Eli whispered, “Where is it?”

Mara looked toward the empty horizon. “That,” she said, “is what we must discover.”

They climbed to the lantern room.

The great lens had stopped turning years ago, when steamships abandoned the northern passage, but the chamber still offered a view in every direction. Sea surrounded them. To the west, the sun was a pale coin behind clouds. To the north, something dark rose and vanished between the waves—perhaps a rock, perhaps a seal.

Eli pressed both hands to the glass. “Could it have sunk?”

“Not without noise.”

“An earthquake?”

“We would have felt it.”

“A storm?”

“There was no storm.”

He turned to her, frightened. “Then how?”

Mara did not answer. She was staring at the shelf beneath the western window.

The shelf held her maps of the island: three hundred and twelve sheets collected over a lifetime. Harbor maps. Field maps. Geological surveys. Old military charts. Children’s drawings of secret paths. A charcoal plan of the monastery made before its roof collapsed. Every map showed the island differently, but all agreed that it existed.

Now the sheets were blank.

Mara crossed the room slowly and lifted the first page.

Nothing.

The ink had not faded. It was gone. The paper looked new.

She pulled out another, then another. Blank. Blank. Blank.

Eli opened a drawer and found the same emptiness. “All of them?”

“Not all,” Mara said.

She hurried downstairs.

On her worktable lay the unfinished map from that morning. Blackhook Point remained where she had drawn it. Fisherman’s Bay curved beneath it. A few thin lines marked the northern roads. But south of the bay, the page was empty because Mara had not yet reached that part.

The ink she had laid down before dawn remained.

She touched the western cliffs with one finger.

“I drew this today,” she said. “After the island vanished.”

Eli stared. “From memory.”

“Yes.”

“So the old maps forgot, but you didn’t.”

“Not yet.”

The words left a chill in the room.

Eli sat heavily. “My mother is down there.”

Mara looked at him.

“In the village,” he continued. “She was making bread. I could smell it when I came up the road. I said I’d return for breakfast.”

His face tightened, but he would not cry. He had always treated tears as if they were expensive.

“She was there,” Mara said. “The village was there.”

“Where are they now?”

“I don’t know.”

“Are they dead?”

“I don’t know.”

“Can we bring them back?”

Mara looked at the half-drawn map.

“That,” she said, “I intend to find out.”

They worked through the morning.

Mara drew while Eli searched the lighthouse for records. They found logbooks with blank pages, tax lists containing no names, and a parish calendar in which every holy day remained but every local festival had vanished.

At noon, Eli discovered something in an old cupboard: a child’s wooden horse painted blue. One wheel was missing.

“My father made this,” he said. “When I was six.”

Mara remembered. Eli had dragged it everywhere for a year, even along the cliffs. He had lost the wheel near the abandoned monastery and cried until his father promised to carve another. His father died before he could do so.

“Objects remember,” Mara said.

“Paper doesn’t?”

“Perhaps paper remembers only what is written on it. And perhaps someone—or something—has erased the island from every record.”

“But not from us.”

“Not yet.”

Again that phrase.

By early afternoon, the edge of Fisherman’s Bay was finished. Mara drew the first houses of the village: the baker’s cottage, the blacksmith’s yard, the inn with its sloping roof. She worked from memory, adding doors, wells, garden walls, and the narrow square where fishermen repaired their nets.

As she drew, the sea outside changed.

Eli noticed first.

“There,” he said, pointing from the window.

A stone chimney rose from the water.

It stood alone, black and dripping, perhaps half a mile east of the lighthouse. Then a rooftop emerged beneath it, water pouring from red tiles. A second roof followed, then a wall, then the top of an apple tree shivering with silver streams.

Mara’s pen stopped.

Far below, where moments before there had been only waves, the upper village was returning.

“Keep going,” Eli breathed.

Mara drew.

The island rose with every line.

Roads appeared as ridges beneath the water. Fields surfaced in shining rectangles. Trees shook themselves like wet dogs. The church steeple climbed from the sea, followed by the bell tower, though the bell made no sound.

But no people appeared.

Eli ran to the door. “Mother!”

Mara caught his arm. “Wait.”

“The road is back.”

“Part of it.”

“I can reach the village.”

“And if it disappears again?”

He pulled against her grip. “She might be there.”

“She is not. Look.”

The village stood drenched and silent. No figures moved between the houses. No smoke rose. The returned island seemed less like a place restored than a stage rebuilt after the actors had gone.

Eli’s anger broke suddenly.

“You’re drawing too slowly.”

Mara released him.

“I’m drawing accurately,” she said.

“I don’t care about the shape of every garden wall!”

“You should.”

“Why?”

“Because we do not know what happens if I draw something incorrectly.”

Eli looked through the door toward the distant roofs.

Mara softened her voice. “Bring me the wooden horse.”

He did.

She placed it beside the map. Then she drew the lane where Eli had lived, his small white house, and the workshop his father had once kept. She drew the fence, the pear tree, and the stone step polished by generations of shoes.

The house rose from the water.

Eli watched, motionless.

There was no one at the window.

“We need more than buildings,” Mara said. “We need names.”

The village archive had vanished, but they remembered enough to begin.

Eli listed families while Mara wrote them into the map’s margins.

Sella Dorn, baker. Tomas Dorn, her brother, missing two fingers on his left hand.

Old Jun at the inn, who watered his ale and denied it.

Nim and Nia Fos, twins who exchanged clothes to confuse strangers.

Father Bell, who had lost his faith but continued ringing the church bell because everyone needed to know the hour.

Lio Marr, fisherman, terrible singer.

Anne Marr, his wife, excellent liar.

Children. Farmers. Sailors. Widows. Babies.

With every name, the air changed. Smoke began rising from chimneys. A dog barked somewhere near the square. The church bell gave a single uncertain note.

Then Eli shouted, “There!”

A figure stood outside the bakery.

She was a broad woman with flour-white hands and a red scarf tied over her hair. She looked around in confusion, then lifted her face toward the lighthouse.

“Mum!”

Eli ran.

This time Mara did not stop him.

He raced down the twelve bends, slipping twice on the wet road. His mother ran uphill to meet him. Even from the lighthouse, Mara heard their cries when they reached each other.

More villagers appeared as Mara wrote. Some emerged from houses. Others stood in fields or on roads, looking dazed. They remembered a strange darkness, a sensation of falling without movement, and a voice speaking just beyond understanding.

By sunset, nearly half the island had returned.

But Mara was exhausted.

Her hand cramped. Her eyes blurred. The pen had worn a sore against her finger, and the room smelled sharply of ink.

The southern half of the map remained empty.

So did the southern half of the island.

Beyond the village, the restored land ended in a clean, impossible line. On one side stood grass, houses, and people. On the other, waves rolled through the place where farms and forests should have been.

The villagers gathered at the lighthouse. Eli and his mother brought food, blankets, and lamps. No one spoke loudly. They seemed afraid noise might draw the attention of whatever had taken them.

Mara sat at her table and drank broth while the village council argued nearby.

“We should evacuate,” said Captain Rusk, who owned the largest fishing boat.

“To where?” asked Father Bell.

“The mainland.”

“The channel is thirty miles. Half the boats are gone with the southern harbor.”

“We can fit everyone if we make two journeys.”

“And if the rest of the island vanishes while you’re at sea?”

Silence followed.

At last Sella Dorn approached Mara. “Can you finish tonight?”

“I can try.”

“Then try.”

Eli bristled. “She’s been drawing since dawn.”

“My daughter is still missing,” Sella said.

Eli’s anger vanished.

Mara remembered Sella’s daughter: Anya, twelve years old, with a laugh so loud it startled birds from roofs. She had been visiting an aunt on a southern farm.

“I’ll draw through the night,” Mara said.

The villagers supplied memories.

They described the south in fragments: a crooked barn, a circle of standing stones, a bridge with blue rails, a pond where white frogs sang in spring. Mara assembled their recollections into lines.

Yet the farther south she went, the harder the drawing became.

Her pen resisted the paper.

At first she blamed fatigue. Then the resistance grew stronger, as if the page had become rough stone. The ink gathered at the nib but refused to flow.

A cold wind moved through the lighthouse, though every window was shut.

The lamps flickered.

Across the unfinished map, words appeared in gray script.

LET IT GO.

The villagers stepped back.

Mara leaned closer. “Who are you?”

The writing faded. New words formed.

THE SEA KEEPS WHAT IS FORGOTTEN.

“We have not forgotten.”

YOU WILL.

Mara set the pen to the page.

Pain shot through her hand. The nib snapped.

At once, the lighthouse shook. Outside, screams rose from the village. The edge of the restored island had begun to crumble—not like earth beneath waves, but like charcoal erased by an unseen thumb.

“Stop!” Eli cried.

Mara seized another pen and wrote in the margin:

I remember.

The shaking ceased.

For several breaths, nothing moved.

Then the answer appeared.

YOU REMEMBER BECAUSE I ALLOW IT.

Mara felt a presence behind the words: ancient, patient, and utterly certain. It was not the sea itself, nor death, nor time, but something that lived where those powers overlapped. A keeper of lost things. A collector of unvisited rooms, nameless graves, abandoned songs, and roads no living feet walked anymore.

“Why this island?” whispered Father Bell.

The paper answered.

NO SHIP COMES. NO KING CLAIMS IT. NO CHART NAMES IT. THE WORLD HAS TURNED AWAY.

Captain Rusk swore. “We live here.”

FOR A LITTLE WHILE.

Mara understood then.

For years, fewer ships had passed. Young people had left for mainland cities. Letters arrived less often. The kingdom’s newest maps omitted the island to make space for trade routes. Even the lighthouse had gone dark because officials decided the northern passage no longer mattered.

The island had not vanished in a single morning.

It had been disappearing for years.

That morning was simply when forgetting became complete.

Mara looked at the people crowding her room. They were frightened, weary, and alive. They had birthdays, grudges, recipes, debts, jokes, scars, and promises. The world’s neglect could not make them unreal.

But perhaps it could make them vulnerable.

“What do you want?” Mara asked.

A final sentence formed.

ONE MEMORY FOR ANOTHER.

Sella grasped Mara’s shoulder. “Don’t.”

Mara barely heard her.

“What memory?”

The answer came slowly.

THE MAPMAKER KNOWS THE ISLAND. GIVE ME THAT KNOWLEDGE, AND THE ISLAND MAY REMAIN.

Eli stared. “It wants your memories.”

“All of them,” Mara said.

She imagined the cost.

Blackhook Point. Fisherman’s Bay. The monastery ruins under snow. Summer markets in the square. Her husband, Jan, laughing as he climbed the lighthouse stairs with flowers stolen from her own garden. Their daughter sleeping in a basket by the window. The fever that took them both in the same winter. The years afterward, when grief made the island seem unbearable, and the longer years when its stones and tides became the language in which grief finally learned to speak.

If she surrendered the island, would Jan’s face go with it? Would she remember loving someone without knowing where they had walked together? Would she remember a child without the room where the child was born?

“You can’t,” Eli said.

Mara looked at him. “There are hundreds of lives at stake.”

“We’ll find another way.”

“We have until the ink dries.”

“Then give it my memories.”

“You don’t know the whole island.”

“I know enough.”

“No.” Mara touched his cheek. “You know the beginning of your life here. I know the end of mine.”

He began to cry then, despite the expense.

Mara turned back to the map.

“I agree,” she said.

The lamps went out.

Darkness filled the lighthouse, but the map shone with a faint blue light. Its unfinished southern coast drew itself beneath Mara’s hands. Forests spread in delicate green strokes. Roads uncoiled. Houses, farms, cliffs, and coves appeared. Names burned briefly in gold.

Outside, the island rose.

The southern fields lifted from the water under streaming moonlight. The old forest surfaced, every branch glittering. Cattle appeared in pastures. Boats settled into the harbor as softly as leaves. The standing stones broke through the waves, followed by the blue bridge, the pond, and Sella’s daughter running barefoot along a muddy road.

The villagers rushed outside, cheering.

Mara remained seated.

Something moved through her mind with the softness of a turning page.

She forgot the taste of apples from the western orchard.

She forgot the bells tied to fishing nets in winter.

She forgot where the white frogs sang.

She forgot Jan’s favorite path.

One by one, the island’s places went dark within her.

She tried to hold on. For an instant she saw Jan beside the ruined monastery, young and sunburned, asking if she believed maps should show where a person had been happiest.

Then the monastery vanished.

Jan stood in empty whiteness.

Then he vanished too.

Mara lowered her head.

By dawn, the island had completely returned.

Sunlight fell across wet roofs. The sea withdrew to its proper shores. People found one another in fields and lanes. Families laughed, wept, and counted their missing.

Not one person had been lost.

In the lighthouse, Eli found Mara asleep over the finished map.

He touched her shoulder.

She woke and looked at him politely.

“Good morning,” she said. “Are you the keeper?”

His face crumpled, but he forced a smile. “No. I’m Eli.”

“Eli,” she repeated. “That’s a good name.”

“Do you know where you are?”

She looked around the circular room, at the windows, instruments, shelves, and sea.

“A lighthouse?”

“Yes.”

“On what coast?”

He swallowed.

“An island,” he said.

Mara studied the map beneath her hands.

It was the finest chart she had ever made. Every path was clear, every reef measured, every house named. In one corner she had drawn a tiny lighthouse and, beside it, a woman at a desk.

Under the figure were four words:

MARA VENN REMEMBERED THIS.

She read the sentence twice.

“Who is Mara Venn?”

“You are.”

“I see.”

She sounded unconvinced.

Eli sat beside her. Outside, the village bells began ringing—not to mark the hour, but because Father Bell had decided the island needed noise.

In the weeks that followed, ships departed in every direction.

Captain Rusk sailed to the mainland carrying copies of Mara’s map. Sella sent loaves stamped with the island’s name. Children wrote letters to newspapers, universities, distant relatives, and the king. Fishermen painted the island’s shape on their sails. Father Bell composed a hymn with twelve verses, most of them poor but all of them memorable.

By autumn, new charts named the island again.

Travelers arrived out of curiosity. Scholars came to inspect the impossible map. Merchants returned to the harbor. The lighthouse was relit, and each night its beam crossed the northern passage, declaring at regular intervals: land here, people here, do not forget.

Mara lived in the lighthouse with Eli and Sella.

She never remembered the island.

Every morning she woke surprised by the view. She learned the roads, then forgot them by evening. She met villagers she had known for decades and listened with courteous interest as they introduced themselves again.

They did not mind.

Each brought her a story.

Old Jun told her how she once caught him watering the ale and marked the village well on her map as “the innkeeper’s second brewery.”

The twins told her she had always known which was which but refused to explain how.

Father Bell told her she had climbed the church tower during a storm to sketch the lightning.

Eli told her about the morning the sea came and how she had drawn them all home.

“Was I frightened?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“Was I brave?”

“Yes.”

“Those are not opposites, I suppose.”

“No,” he said. “I don’t think they are.”

Years passed.

Eli became the lighthouse keeper and then, though he still drew crooked coastlines, the island’s mapmaker. He trained children to measure roads and taught sailors to read the stars. Above his desk hung Mara’s final map in a frame of black oak.

Visitors often asked why the island needed so many maps when one would surely be enough.

Eli always answered the same way.

“One map can be lost.”

Mara grew old. On clear days, she sat outside the lighthouse wrapped in a blue blanket, watching ships enter the harbor.

Sometimes travelers recognized her. They thanked her for saving a place she could no longer name. She accepted their gratitude with amused embarrassment.

Near the end of her life, Eli carried her to Blackhook Point.

The western cliffs shone red in the sunset. Below, the sea struck the rocks and burst into white spray. Gulls floated on the rising wind.

Mara looked out for a long time.

“This place is beautiful,” she said.

“It was always your favorite.”

“Was it?”

“Yes.”

She considered that and smiled. “Then I had good taste.”

Eli laughed.

Far across the water, the lighthouse beam awakened and swept over the darkening sea. In the village, bells rang the hour. Doors opened. Lamps appeared in windows one by one, each small light holding its ground against the night.

Mara watched them.

“I feel,” she said slowly, “as if I have been here before.”

Eli took her hand.

“You have.”

She nodded, satisfied.

Together they remained on the cliff until the stars came out and the whole island, mapped and named and remembered, shone beneath them.
